what_it_does: Neural networks do enormous numbers of multiply-and-add operations (the core arithmetic of matrix multiplication). One way to speed these up is to notice that many of the weight values contain runs of zero bits, so those individual bit-level multiplications can be skipped — this is called bit-level sparsity (exploiting the fact that many bits in the numbers are zero). This technique works well on custom silicon chips (ASICs — application-specific integrated circuits built for one purpose), but implementing it on FPGAs (programmable chips whose logic can be rewired after manufacture) is harder because FPGA logic blocks (lookup tables, or LUTs) have fixed structures that do not naturally map to variable-length sparse operations. This paper presents a software-hardware co-design — changes to both the way weights are encoded and the hardware circuits — so that bit-level sparsity maps cleanly onto FPGA logic. The encoding is designed to fit naturally into LUTs, and the hardware can tolerate that some multiply operations finish faster than others (because they skip more bits), which is a timing challenge the design explicitly handles.
